title: Bavan Akhri close
hookLine: a long alphabet ending in grace

lines: A SLATE AT THE END OF THE DAY.
THE LAST MARK IS A GIFT.
cards: A school slate at the end of the day. Chalk dust in the corners, a row of letters copied over and over, a teacher's mark at the bottom.
Guru Arjan's Bavan Akhri in Raga Gauri works like that slate, stretched across the Guru Granth Sahib from Ang two hundred fifty. Letter after letter, each one opens a lesson.
Today, the bottom of the slate, where the teacher leaves the last mark. And the last mark isn't a grade. It's a gift.

teach.b: An acrostic sets up an expectation. Each letter is a step, and steps sound like effort: learn this, then this, and you'll arrive.

The Bavan Akhri uses that shape, and along the way it says hard things, like the sassa stanza's warning about cleverness that goes nowhere. You'd expect the ending to reward the student who finished every letter.
Instead, as this path reads it, a long alphabet ends in grace.

teach.h: THE CLOSE TURNS TO THE GIVER.
teach.b: The close turns from the student to the Giver: the Name comes through the Lord's mercy and the Guru's kindness, not through anyone's own cleverness. Sikh vocabulary has words for that turn.
Kirpa is mercy, kindness given freely. Nadar is the gracious glance, the Lord looking with favor. Sikh teaching holds both together with effort.
Sikhs are asked to rise, remember, work honestly, serve, and Gurbani speaks of the fruit of all that as a gift. Some readers hear the whole composition as a lesson in the right order of things.
Then you find out who was holding the chalk. So the long schoolroom poem doesn't end by praising the pupil.
It ends with the pupil looking up: the work was real, and the gift was bigger than the work.

how: The Bavan Akhri of Guru Arjan is part of the Guru Granth Sahib in Raga Gauri; some Sikhs read it through in their own study or hear it explained in katha at the gurdwara.

games.q: you've worked through a long lesson, letter by letter. the teacher reaches the bottom of the slate. what does the Bavan Akhri's close do?
o: hand out a grade for the work done.
turn the pupil toward the Giver and speak of grace.
start the alphabet again from the first letter.
games.why: the long alphabet ends in grace: the work was real, and the gift was bigger than the work.

practice: If you have a gutka, an app or a printed Guru Granth Sahib nearby, find the closing lines of the Bavan Akhri in Raga Gauri and read them once, slowly, in Gurmukhi or in translation.

If not, sit with one thing you worked hard for this year and notice how much of it was also given: a teacher, a chance, a person who said yes. Hold both, the work and the gift, and if you pray, close with a quiet Waheguru.
